consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same core: the fear of the LORD is reverent awe and humble respect toward God that produces obedience, worship, and the shunning of evil, and is the foundation of wisdom (Prov 1:7; 9:10; Eccl 12:13). Alternatives (servile dread, covenant loyalty, filial fear, gift of the Spirit) are treated as complementary emphases rather than rival cores.
book_summary: The book defines fear of the LORD as reverent awe that produces obedience, turning a person from evil and toward keeping the LORD's commandments, citing Ecclesiastes 12:13.
consensus_core_identification: Reverent awe/respect toward God that issues in obedience and avoidance of evil, foundational to wisdom.
book_core_identification: Reverent awe producing obedience — turning from evil and toward God's commandments.
boundary_disagreement: None. The book's phrasing ('reverent awe that produces obedience... turns from evil') tracks the consensus definition almost word for word; it neither narrows the term to servile dread nor broadens it beyond the standard reverence-obedience reading.
rationale: The book's core identification is a compact restatement of the consensus: reverent awe as the disposition, obedience and turning from evil as its fruit. Every blind response names exactly these elements as the primary meaning (e.g., Response B: 'reverence... which leads to obedience... and the shunning of evil'). No boundary, condition, or extension differs; nothing in the entry rejects or reclassifies any case the consensus admits. Hence MATCH with equivalent cores and identical extension.
strongest_objection: One could argue the single printed citation (Eccl 12:13) supports the obedience component ('Fear God, and keep his commandments') but does not itself establish 'reverent awe' rather than dread, nor the 'turning from evil' clause (which rests on Prov 8:13, 16:6, Job 28:28, uncited). This weakens citation support but does not create any substantive disagreement with the consensus definition.
